docs.title: EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves
docs.text: Credits: 3 (3 lecture hours per week) Level: Undergraduate, junior year Prerequisites: Circuit analysis I and II; vector calculus (multivariable calculus); university physics II (electricity and magnetism) Corequisite (recommended): Differential equations

docs.title: Catalog Description
docs.text: An introduction to electromagnetic fields and waves for electrical engineers, starting with transmission lines and building up to Maxwell's equations and plane waves. Topics include wave propagation on transmission lines, impedance matching and the Smith chart, transients on lines, electrostatics and magnetostatics, Maxwell's equations, uniform plane waves, reflection and transmission at boundaries, and an introduction to waveguides and antennas. Applications cover high-speed digital interconnects, RF and microwave circuits, and wireless and optical systems.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text: At high frequencies, or when interconnects are long relative to the signal's wavelength, ordinary circuit theory stops working: voltage and current turn into traveling waves. EE3601 bridges circuit analysis and field theory. It starts with transmission lines, where wave behavior can be studied with familiar circuit quantities, and then develops the field theory underneath it. Students learn to analyze, design and match transmission-line circuits and to predict how electromagnetic waves propagate, reflect and transmit in practical engineering systems.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
1. Introduction to waves and phasors. Traveling waves, wavelength, phase velocity; when circuit theory breaks down; review of phasors and complex numbers.
  2. Transmission-line theory. Distributed-element model; telegrapher's equations; characteristic impedance; propagation constant; lossless and low-loss lines.
  3. Terminated transmission lines. Reflection coefficient; standing waves and VSWR; input impedance; short-circuited, open-circuited and quarter-wave lines; power flow.
  4. The Smith chart and impedance matching. Smith chart construction and use; lumped-element (L-section) matching; single-stub matching; quarter-wave transformers.
  5. Transients on transmission lines. Step and pulse response; bounce diagrams; reflections in digital interconnects and signal integrity.
  6. Vector analysis review. Coordinate systems; gradient, divergence and curl; the divergence and Stokes theorems.
  7. Electrostatics. Coulomb's law; Gauss's law; electric potential; conductors and dielectrics; boundary conditions; capacitance; Laplace's and Poisson's equations.
  8. Magnetostatics. Biot–Savart law; Ampère's law; magnetic flux and vector potential; magnetic materials; inductance.
  9. Maxwell's equations. Faraday's law; displacement current; Maxwell's equations in integral and differential (point) form; time-harmonic fields; boundary conditions.
  10. Uniform plane waves. The wave equation; propagation in lossless and lossy media; skin depth; polarization; the Poynting vector and power density.
  11. Reflection and transmission of plane waves. Normal and oblique incidence; Snell's law; Fresnel coefficients; total internal reflection; Brewster angle.
  12. Introduction to waveguides and antennas. Rectangular waveguides, TE and TM modes, and cutoff frequency; radiation from a Hertzian dipole; basic antenna parameters.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  1. Decide when wave effects matter in a circuit and model the interconnect as a transmission line.
  2. Calculate the voltage, current, impedance, reflection coefficient, VSWR and power flow on terminated transmission lines.
  3. Use the Smith chart to analyze impedances and design lumped-element, stub and quarter-wave matching networks.
  4. Analyze transient signals on transmission lines with bounce diagrams and explain how reflections affect signal integrity.
  5. Apply Gauss's, Ampère's and Faraday's laws to find static and time-varying fields and to calculate capacitance and inductance.
  6. State Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form and explain the physical meaning of each.
  7. Describe how uniform plane waves propagate in lossless and lossy media, including attenuation, skin depth, polarization and power density.
  8. Calculate the reflection and transmission of plane waves at boundaries between media, for both normal and oblique incidence.
  9. Explain guided-wave propagation in waveguides and the basic principles of radiation from antennas.

docs.title: Assessment (suggested)
docs.text: Component Weight Homework 20% Quizzes 10% Computational / lab projects (e.g., Smith chart, TDR measurements, field simulation) 15% Midterm exams (2) 30% Final exam 25%

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text: Course: EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves File assessed: docs/course-description.md Analyzer version: 0.05 Date: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Overall Score: 68/100
docs.text:
Quality rating: Adequate — several improvements needed before learning graph generation.

The topic coverage is detailed and technically precise, and on its own it could support well over 200 concepts. The score is held back by structure, not substance: the nine learning outcomes are one flat list rather than being grouped by the six levels of the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy, and the description never states what the course does not cover.

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Earned Notes Title 5 5 "EE3601 — Transmission Lines, Fields, and Waves" is clear and descriptive. Target Audience 5 5 "Undergraduate, junior year" — specific. Prerequisites 5 5 Circuit analysis I and II, vector calculus, physics II; differential equations as a corequisite. Main Topics Covered 10 10 Twelve topics, each with a detailed list of subtopics. Topics Excluded 5 0 There is no section that sets the course's boundaries. Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "By the end of the course, students will be able to:" is present. Remember Level 10 4 Only one outcome is recall-oriented ("State Maxwell's equations…", #6). Understand Level 10 8 Three outcomes fit (#6, #7, #9: explain, describe, explain), but they are not labeled as this level. Apply Level 10 9 Strong: #2, #3, #5 and #8 (calculate, use, apply). Not labeled. Analyze Level 10 5 One clear outcome (#4: analyze transients with bounce diagrams). Evaluate Level 10 3 Only #1 ("decide when wave effects matter") involves judgment. No outcomes about comparing or justifying design choices. Create Level 10 4 Only #3 includes design (matching networks). No capstone or open-ended design project is described. Descriptive Context 5 5 The course overview explains clearly why circuit theory breaks down and why this course matters. Total 100 68

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. No topics-excluded section (0/5). Without boundaries, the learning graph generator may pull in neighboring subjects: full antenna design, numerical methods (FDTD and finite elements), optical fibers, quantum electrodynamics, or the derivation of special relativity. Each of these wastes concept slots and distorts the dependency graph.
  2. Remember level is thin (4/10). The learning graph needs foundational "leaf" concepts: units, constants (ε₀, μ₀, c, η₀), definitions, and named laws. With only one recall outcome, the generator has less signal for which basics to list explicitly.
  3. Evaluate level is thin (3/10). Engineering judgment is a real goal of this course (which matching network? is the line electrically long? which cable meets the loss budget?), but the outcomes barely express it.
  4. Create level lacks a capstone (4/10). The assessment table mentions computational and lab projects, but no outcome describes what students build. Without one, the graph has few integrative "goal" concepts at the top.
  5. Analyze level is thin (5/10). Field problems invite analysis outcomes, such as breaking a geometry into symmetric regions to choose a Gaussian surface or Amperian loop, but only transient analysis is listed.
  6. The outcomes aren't grouped by Bloom level. Even the strong outcomes aren't labeled by level, so later skills (quiz-generator, chapter content) can't target specific cognitive levels.

docs.title: 1. Restructure the learning outcomes by Bloom's level (highest impact)
docs.text:
Keep the nine existing outcomes, but sort them under six headings and add 3–5 outcomes where a level is thin. Examples:

Remember

  • Recall the values and units of ε₀, μ₀, the speed of light c, and the intrinsic impedance of free space η₀ ≈ 377 Ω.
  • List Maxwell's four equations and the constitutive relations.
  • Identify the parts of a Smith chart: constant-resistance circles, constant-reactance arcs, and the wavelength scale.
  • Name common transmission-line types (coaxial, two-wire, microstrip, stripline) and their typical characteristic impedances.

Understand

  • Explain why circuit theory fails when a line is long compared with a wavelength.
  • Interpret standing-wave patterns in terms of incident and reflected waves.
  • Describe the physical meaning of displacement current.
  • Explain skin depth and why it limits conductor thickness at high frequencies.

Apply — keep the current #2, #3, #5 and #8.

Analyze

  • Analyze transients with bounce diagrams (current #4).
  • Choose a Gaussian surface or Amperian loop by examining a problem's symmetry.
  • Break a lossy-media problem into attenuation and phase contributions.
  • Diagnose the location and type of a fault from a time-domain reflectometry (TDR) trace.

Evaluate

  • Decide when wave effects matter (current #1).
  • Compare lumped-element, single-stub, and quarter-wave matching for a given bandwidth and frequency, and justify a choice.
  • Evaluate whether a PCB trace needs termination given its rise time and length.
  • Judge whether the low-loss approximation is valid for a given line or medium.

Create

  • Design a matching network for a given load and verify it in simulation or on a vector network analyzer.
  • Design a termination scheme for a high-speed digital bus that meets a reflection budget.
  • Capstone idea: design, simulate and measure a microstrip interconnect with a matching network, including a TDR characterization and a short written design justification.

docs.title: 2. Add a "Topics Not Covered" section
docs.text:
Suggested boundaries:

  • Antenna array design and advanced antenna synthesis (only the Hertzian dipole and basic antenna parameters are covered)
  • Numerical electromagnetics (FDTD, method of moments, finite element method), apart from using a field solver as a tool
  • Optical fiber modes and photonics beyond plane-wave reflection and refraction
  • Circular and dielectric waveguides, resonant cavities
  • Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) regulation and shielding design
  • Relativistic electrodynamics and quantum electrodynamics

docs.title: 3. Optionally, name the computational tools
docs.text: Naming the tools (for example, Python or MATLAB, a field solver, a Smith chart tool) gives the generator concrete skill concepts to list in the graph.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Factor Assessment Topic breadth 12 topics spanning circuits, statics, dynamics, and waves — excellent Topic depth Each topic lists 4–8 named subtopics — excellent Diversity of concept types Definitions, laws, quantities, tools (Smith chart), procedures (matching), and applications — good Estimated concept count About 250–320 concepts from the topic list alone (≈ 20–25 per topic)

The description already has enough material for 200+ concepts. The improvements above matter less for the concept count than for the graph's shape. Clear boundaries keep the graph from sprawling, and Bloom-level outcomes give it well-defined foundational concepts at the bottom and integrative goals at the top.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
The score is below 85, so revise the course description before running learning-graph-generator:

  1. Regroup the learning outcomes by the six Bloom's Taxonomy levels, adding the suggested outcomes for Remember, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create.
  2. Add a "Topics Not Covered" section.
  3. Re-run course-description-analyzer. With both changes the description should score about 90 or higher.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).
